questions.question: Is the reported Spearman computed per group and averaged, weighted by group size or pair count, or pooled across all observations?
questions.rationale: Pooling mixes within-group order with cross-group score offsets, which a translation-invariant ranking loss never pins down ([Yan et al. 2022](https://research.google/pubs/scale-calibration-of-deep-ranking-models/)). A per-group average gives a two-item group, which carries one bit, the same weight as a 25-item group with 300 pairs (inference).
questions.interpretation: **Pooled:** part of both numbers measures the cross-group calibration of a head that was never trained for it. Evaluate the BCE logit or an anchored score instead. **Per-group average:** the value is driven by groups of two or three, so compare it with a pair-weighted concordance before reading anything into the plateau.
questions.answer: The required selection metric eval_macro_spearman is the unweighted mean of eligible, defined per-assay Spearman correlations. eval_spearman aliases the observation-count-weighted mean; neither pools scores across observations and neither weights by pair count. Historical illustrative 0.41/0.20 numbers in the spec are not assumed to be matched macro results.

questions.question: Which groups enter the metric? How are size-one groups, constant groups and ties created by median aggregation handled? Does the eligible fraction differ between splits?
questions.rationale: Spearman is undefined for constant groups. The median of an even number of replicates can create exact ties. An eligibility rule that differs from the training rule scores pairs the loss ignored.
questions.interpretation: If the eligible fraction or tie rate differs between the two test partitions, part of the gap is compositional rather than a failure to generalize.
questions.answer: The actual headline requires n>=3 and pChEMBL span>=0.5, excludes constant labels, and uses average ranks for exact ties. Size-one and size-two assays are excluded. Constant predictions produce undefined rho, excluded with defined coverage recorded. A test has 8278/16431 eligible assays (50.38%); B has 3972/9578 (41.47%). Headline labels are float32 tensor values promoted to Python float. The raw exported float64 B test labels instead admit 3971 assays; correcting that precision reproduces the native test macro exactly (0.1768796098004701) on identical saved scores.

questions.question: What is the replicate-based noise ceiling of the chosen metric on each split?
questions.rationale: A noise ceiling marks the point where "any remaining mismatch is then attributable to the noise in the measurements" ([Nili et al. 2014](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3990488)). The replicates that are currently aggregated by median make it computable: split each pair's replicates into halves, score one half against the other with the headline metric, and apply a Spearman–Brown correction.
questions.interpretation: If Split B's ceiling is lower, part of the gap is a difference in measurement quality, and the right report is the fraction of the ceiling reached. Two caveats apply. Spearman–Brown assumes parallel measurements ([SAGE](https://sk.sagepub.com/ency/edvol/embed/the-sage-encyclopedia-of-research-design-2e/chpt/spearman-brown-prophecy-formula)), and this research found no ML precedent for a noise ceiling on a grouped rank metric.
questions.answer: Test split-half macro Spearman is A 0.5445 versus B 0.3780; the requested Spearman-Brown heuristic is A 0.7050 versus B 0.5485. Coverage is only 420/8278 (5.07%) and 348/3972 (8.76%) eligible assays, respectively. These conditional heuristics do not establish a ceiling or fraction-of-ceiling result for the entire test set.

questions.question: How does within-group variance of s divide among the y-cluster main effect, the x×y interaction, and replicate noise?

Cross-attention can only add value on the interaction share (inference).
questions.interpretation: A small interaction share means Split A's 0.41 rested largely on y main effects that do not transfer across similarity regions. In that case 0.20 sits near the cold-y limit for any architecture (hypothesis). Because most y are seen about twice, fit the model at the y-cluster level.
questions.answer: The requested raw-measurement variance model and an assay-balanced sensitivity fit are complete, but the decomposition is unstable. A test within-assay interaction contribution changes from 0 to 0.1159204 pChEMBL squared; B changes from 0.1716375 to 0.0567531. Training noise estimates conflict with direct replicate disagreement. A stable interaction share or architectural ceiling is not established; raw noise is not median-label uncertainty.

questions.question: Does the contrastive loss treat other positives of the same x in the batch as negatives?
questions.rationale: With group batching and diagonal-only targets, a positive anchor in a 25-item group at 70% positives sees about 16–17 labeled positives as negatives (inference). questions.interpretation: If co-positives are treated as negatives, the contrastive loss directly opposes the BCE and ranking losses. Masking them, or using multi-positive targets, is the first fix to test.
questions.answer: The reference already hides own-assay co-candidates and masks cross-assay same-protein and duplicate-query-molecule entries. Those observed same-protein negatives are zero in the audit. Global training-known positives can remain negatives when sampled under another protein. Across 512 deterministic epoch-zero batches per split, these are 0.530%/0.714% of protein-to-molecule negative comparisons on A/B (0.437/0.576 per active anchor), and 0.441%/0.657% in the reverse direction. A gradient fixture verifies their negative push. questions.question: Are the contrastive projections taken before or after cross-attention?
questions.rationale: Pair-independent embeddings allow cheap in-batch negatives and a full softmax over all 8,000 x. Pair-dependent embeddings require recomputing cross-attention for every off-diagonal pair.
questions.interpretation: This architectural detail determines which contrastive remedies are feasible.
questions.answer: Before cross-attention. In the reference mlp_contrastive mode, separate protein and molecule projections consume pooled encoder outputs and produce normalized, pair-independent embeddings. Ranking and BCE consume fused representations. Cross-pair contrastive scores therefore require embedding products, not new cross-attention passes.

questions.question: How is the listwise loss normalized across groups of different sizes?
questions.rationale: Summing over pairs lets the roughly 10% of large groups dominate the gradient. Per-group averaging matches a per-group-averaged metric (inference).
questions.interpretation: If loss weighting and metric weighting differ, the model is optimizing groups the metric barely counts.
questions.answer: The reference sums top-weighted Plackett-Luce selections within each sampled list, with tie-averaged weights 1/(sqrt(list size)*log(position+1)), then averages sampled lists. It does not divide by the retained selection-weight sum. Larger original assays receive ceil(n/32) bounded ranking-list opportunities, so this is not equal weighting of original assays. The controlled comparison separately implements within-list normalization and inverse-opportunity assay balancing without changing sampled rows or update counts.

questions.interpretation: A strong x-popularity component in the contrastive branch is a shortcut that needs no information about y.

This establishes skewed candidate frequency, not that the learned contrastive score actually uses a popularity shortcut; that requires pathway/probe evidence.
